title: How AI Is Changing Every Role on a Software Team
summary: AI now drafts the docs, code and tests. What's left for BAs, POs, PMs, designers, devs and QA is framing, judging and owning the result. A role-by-role look.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say a BA pastes three meeting transcripts into a chat window and gets twelve neat user stories back in under a minute. They read well: acceptance criteria, edge cases, the lot. Two of them, though, describe a refund flow the business dropped last year. Nobody spots it until QA files a bug two sprints later.

That little scene is most of the story of AI on a software team right now. The draft got cheap. Knowing whether the draft is right did not. This post goes role by role (BA, PO, PM, designer, developer, QA and a few more) and asks the same three things each time: what's fading, what's growing and what can bite you. The numbers come from studies you can open and check yourself, and I've noted when I checked them.

Who this is for

Anyone whose work touches how software gets made: finding out what people need, deciding what to build, building it, or making sure it holds up. You don't need to write code to get something out of this.

The one shift under all the others

Strip away the job titles and one pattern repeats. For decades the slow part of software was producing things: the spec, the code, the test plan, the mockup. AI now produces first versions of all of these in seconds. So the slow part moves. It moves to saying clearly what you want, steering the work and checking what comes back.

A big industry survey points the same way. For its 2025 report (published September 2025), Google's DORA team surveyed nearly 5,000 tech professionals. 90% used AI at work and more than 80% felt it made them more productive. Yet more AI adoption went with higher delivery throughput and lower delivery stability. DORA's reading is that AI amplifies what a team already has: more changes flow out, and weak tests or slow feedback loops downstream start to show (Google Cloud, announcing the 2025 DORA report).

Feeling faster and being faster are also different things. In METR's early-2025 study, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in repos they knew well. With AI tools (mostly Cursor with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet at the time) they took 19% longer, and afterward they believed AI had sped them up by 20% (METR, July 2025). METR has since said those results no longer reflect current tools. Its February 2026 follow-up thinks developers are probably faster now, but calls its own data "only very weak evidence" for how much (METR, February 2026; checked November 2026). The lesson survives the update: your gut is a poor stopwatch.

There's a knock-on effect too. When a feature took a month, a weak idea usually died in planning. When it takes an afternoon, the weak idea ships. As building gets cheaper, building the wrong thing costs more, and good judgment about what to build is worth more.

The skill under every role

What you get out of a model depends heavily on what you put in: background, constraints, what "done" looks like. Designing that input on purpose has a name, context engineering, and every role below needs a bit of it.

Business Analyst (BA)

A BA translates between messy humans and precise systems. AI handles the mechanical half of that well (summarizing, structuring, reformatting). It has no access to the human half: the politics, the unwritten rules, the thing the ops lead mentioned once over lunch.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Writing long requirement docs and first-draft user stories by handFinding the real problem behind the request
Collating research notes and meeting transcriptsAsking the questions stakeholders didn't think to answer
Reformatting the same content for every audienceChecking AI-extracted requirements against how the business really works

More and more, the BA is the person who feeds the model accurate domain knowledge, and the one who notices when a requirement sounds right and isn't.

Watch out

A model will happily write complete, well-structured requirements that are wrong, and the wrong ones look exactly as polished as the right ones. Your value is knowing the business well enough to catch that before it becomes a sprint of work.

Product Owner (PO)

When building gets cheap, deciding what to build gets expensive. That's the PO's whole job.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Backlog chores and acceptance criteria from a blank pagePrioritizing hard and saying no out loud
Compiling stakeholder updatesDefining a good outcome in numbers people can check
First-pass specs and release notesTalking to customers and checking the demand is real
Watch out

The risk is a feature factory with a turbo button: more shipped, faster, in the wrong direction. With building this cheap, checking demand before you commit becomes most of the work. Speed without direction just burns money faster.

Project / Product Manager (PM)

A lot of classic PM work is coordination overhead: status reports, meeting notes, decks, follow-ups. AI is good at exactly that, which leaves more room for the part that was always the real job.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Status reports, meeting summaries, first-draft decksCoordinating people and AI agents toward one outcome
Basic planning and timeline assemblyMaking hard trade-off calls with incomplete information
Chasing people for updates to build reports by handKeeping stakeholders aligned and earning their trust
Watch out

AI makes activity cheap: polished docs, tidy tickets, beautiful plans. None of that proves a decision got made. Keep asking which outcome actually moved this week.

Designer (UX/UI)

Generative tools now turn out mockups, variants and microcopy in seconds. A designer's value moves from making every pixel to directing the work and choosing well.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Pixel-pushing first draftsTaste and a clear point of view
Hand-making dozens of layout and copy variantsTurning user research into design intent
Repetitive component and asset assemblyDesign systems, accessibility and a coherent brand
Watch out

When anyone can generate a passable screen, passable stops being worth much. The difference comes from intent: hierarchy, character, a system that hangs together. Picking from AI options without a point of view just adds more sameness.

Developer / Software Engineer

This is the loudest change and the most misread one. AI writes code fast, but typing was never the hard part. The hard parts were understanding the system, fitting a change into it and proving the change works. That's where the job is heading.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Boilerplate, syntax recall, looking up APIsSystem design and the shape of the whole
First-draft implementation and simple CRUDReading and reviewing far more code than you write
Writing basic, mechanical testsDebugging the subtle stuff and stating intent precisely
Mechanical refactors and ports between frameworksTrade-offs, security and knowing why

The senior question used to be "can you build this?" Now it's closer to "can you tell, quickly and reliably, whether this is correct, safe and maintainable?" That second question is harder than it looks. In a Stanford user study, participants who had an AI code assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without one, and were more likely to believe their code was secure (Perry et al., "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?"). The assistant in that study is older than today's tools. The overconfidence is a human pattern, though, and it's the part to watch.

Watch out

Three traps: skills that fade because you stop practicing them, confident code with a subtle security hole, and code that works while nobody on the team understands it (more on that in cognitive debt). A good habit: treat AI output like a PR from a fast new teammate. Useful, worth reading properly, never merged unread. The code review post has the checklist.

QA / QC Engineer

QA may change the most, because AI both helps testers and hands them a new kind of thing to test: features that don't give the same answer twice.

What's fadingWhat's growing
Running the same manual tests over and overExploratory testing and trying hard to break things
Boilerplate test cases and basic regression scriptsDefining what "quality" means for a feature
Hand-fixing brittle UI scriptsRisk-based thinking: where failure actually hurts
Nothing to replace here. This work is new.Evaluating AI features: writing evals for LLM output, testing for hallucination, bias and safety
Watch out

Two traps. AI-written tests for AI-written code tend to share the same blind spots, so keep some verification independent of the model that wrote the code. And classic pass/fail checks break on non-deterministic output, because a good answer can take many valid forms. That's why evals exist, and QA is well placed to own them. Evaluating LLM performance covers how.

And the rest of the team

The neighboring roles follow the same pattern:

RoleFadingGrowing
DevOps / SREBoilerplate IaC, runbooks, grepping logsReliability of systems with AI inside, compute cost control, observability for agents, guardrails
Data / AnalystSQL from scratch, basic charts, assembling reportsAsking the right question, data quality, statistical judgment, defining metrics
EM / Tech LeadFirst-pass review volume, collecting statusGrowing people while AI does the grunt work, setting the quality bar, deciding where AI fits, keeping a growth path for juniors

What we could lose without noticing

Some losses are pure upside. Nobody misses writing boilerplate. A few are worth naming and protecting on purpose, because they wear away slowly:

  • The junior-to-senior ladder. Juniors grew by doing exactly the tasks AI now absorbs. In January 2026 Anthropic published a randomized trial with 52 mostly junior engineers learning a Python library they had never used. The group with AI averaged 50% on a quiz afterward, against 67% for the group coding by hand, and the biggest gap was on debugging questions. People who used AI to ask conceptual questions scored well. People who handed it the whole task scored lowest (Anthropic, "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills"). The authors point out the sample was small and the quiz came right after the task, but the direction is worth taking seriously.
  • Deep understanding. When code and tests appear instantly, it's tempting to ship what you don't fully get. That debt tends to come due at the worst moment, usually an incident at 2 a.m.
  • Productive struggle. Some skills only form while you wrestle with a hard problem. Hand every struggle to a model and a team can end up fast and shallow.
  • Originality. If you always take the first suggestion, your work starts to look like everyone else's first suggestion.
Automation bias

People tend to over-trust a confident machine. A 2011 systematic review of 74 studies on automation bias pooled four healthcare studies: when the decision support gave wrong advice, people using it were about 26% more likely to make the wrong call than people working without it (Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt, JAMIA). The same review lists stressing personal accountability and training among the things that help. Staying a bit skeptical is just part of the job.

The skills that matter more now

If producing things no longer sets you apart, these do:

  • Context engineering: giving a model the background, constraints and intent it needs to get it right the first time.
  • Verification and evals: judging AI output quickly and reliably, including for features that never answer the same way twice.
  • Taste: knowing what good looks like and being able to say why. When options are free, choosing is the work.
  • Problem framing: shaping a vague need into a clear problem with edges. A model can't do this alone because it doesn't know what you actually want.
  • Orchestration: steering a mix of people and agents toward one outcome, then fitting the pieces together.
  • Systems and security thinking: seeing the whole system, its edges and its failure modes, which is exactly the context a model lacks by default.

AI-assisted vs AI-first

Both phrases get thrown around loosely. Here's a useful way to tell them apart:

  • AI-assisted keeps the old process and adds AI on top. A developer still writes the code and takes autocomplete suggestions. A BA still writes the doc and asks AI to tidy it. Faster, same workflow.
  • AI-first redesigns the process so AI drafts almost everything while people specify, steer and verify. Tooling, rituals and sometimes the roles themselves reshape around that. From SDLC to ADLC looks at what this does to the delivery lifecycle.
Don't copy AI-first blindly

AI-first can be a real advantage when the guardrails come with it: solid review, evals, clear ownership and a plan for how people keep learning. DORA's data hints at what happens without them: change volume goes up and weak tests or slow feedback loops start to show. Go fast, and build the brakes at the same time.

What to keep an eye on

  • Fluent wrong answers. Models state false things in perfect prose. Anything with real consequences (code, requirements, numbers, claims) is a draft to verify. Reducing hallucinations has practical tactics.
  • Ownership. "The AI wrote it" won't hold up in a postmortem. Whoever merges it owns it.
  • Security and data. Generated code can carry vulnerabilities or license problems, and pasted context can leak customer data. Read your company's AI policy before you paste.
  • The evaluation gap. If you can't tell good output from bad, AI just helps you be wrong faster. Build the judging skill before you scale the producing.
  • Sameness. Default output drifts toward the most common pattern. Standing out takes deliberate human intent.

How to adapt, practically

  • Spend your learning time where AI is weak: framing problems, judging trade-offs, verifying, understanding systems and working with people.
  • Treat review as a craft, whatever your role. Practice judging output fast and well.
  • Keep your fundamentals warm. Use AI to go faster, and now and then solve something hard by hand. The Anthropic study suggests that asking the model "why" instead of "do it for me" keeps more of the learning.
  • Learn context engineering on purpose. This guide is a good place to start.
  • If you lead a team, redesign how juniors learn. Pair them on reviews of AI output, ask them to explain a change in their own words before merge, and leave some hard problems for them to wrestle with.
  • Measure instead of guessing. Note cycle time and change failure rate before and after you roll out a tool. The METR study shows how far the gut can drift.

Try this week

  • Pick one AI-drafted thing you shipped last week and check one claim in it against its source.
  • Write down two parts of your role that AI can't do yet, and block an hour for one of them.
  • Next time you use AI on something new to you, ask it to explain the why before you ask for code.
  • If you lead, add "explain this AI-written change in your own words" to your review checklist.
  • Pick one metric (cycle time, change failure rate or rework) and write down today's number so you can compare in a month.

"Will AI take my job?" is the anxious version of a better question: which parts of my job is AI taking, and what's left? For most roles, what's left is deciding what's worth doing and making sure it's done right. That part is growing, and honestly, it was always the fun part.

faqs.q: Will AI replace roles like BA, PM, developer or QA?
faqs.a: So far the evidence points to roles changing shape. AI absorbs specific tasks inside each role, such as first-draft documents, boilerplate code, routine test cases and status reports. What remains is framing problems, judging output and owning the result. The people most exposed are those whose work was only the tasks that are now easy to automate.

faqs.q: What's the most useful skill to build for an AI-first team?
faqs.a: Two skills that work together: giving AI the right context (context engineering) and judging quickly whether its output is correct, safe and good (verification). In every role, the slow part of the work has moved from producing things to specifying them and checking them.

faqs.q: What's the difference between AI-assisted and AI-first?
faqs.a: AI-assisted keeps your current workflow and adds AI to speed up parts of it. AI-first redesigns the workflow so AI drafts most things while people specify, steer and verify. AI-first only pays off with guardrails: solid review, evals, clear ownership and a plan for how people keep learning.

faqs.q: How does AI change QA and testing?
faqs.a: AI automates much of the routine work, like repetitive runs, boilerplate cases and basic regression scripts, which pushes QA toward exploratory and risk-based testing. AI features also give non-deterministic output, so pass/fail checks aren't enough and teams need evals. Keep some verification independent, because AI-written tests for AI-written code tend to share blind spots.

faqs.q: Does AI really make developers faster?
faqs.a: It depends on the setting, and feelings are a poor guide. In METR's early-2025 study, experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with AI tools while believing they were 20% faster. METR's February 2026 follow-up thinks developers are probably faster with newer tools, but calls its data very weak evidence for how much. Measure your own cycle time instead of guessing.
